result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_cycles()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get all elementary cycles in the graph using Johnson's algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21536-L21616){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_cycles(min_length=2) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Elementary cycles (directed)](/assets/graphs/get-cycles.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed graph shaped like a house. Johnson's algorithm finds the two cycles that follow the edge directions: the triangle C, A, B in the accent color and the outer loop C, A, B, D, E in teal. The square B, C, E, D is not a directed cycle." width="100%"} Implements Donald B. Johnson's 1975 algorithm for finding all elementary (simple) cycles in a directed graph. Each cycle is found exactly once and contains no repeated nodes except the first/last. This method only works on directed graphs. For undirected graphs, convert to directed first or consider that every edge forms a 2-cycle. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [min_length]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum cycle length to report. Cycles shorter than this are ignored. The default is `2` (includes self-loops if present). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of cycles, where each cycle is a list of node IDs forming the cycle. The start node is not repeated at the end. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected (cycle enumeration requires directed graphs). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Enumeration is powered by Johnson's algorithm, which runs in $O\!\left((V + E)(C + 1)\right)$ time and $O(V + E)$ space, where $C$ is the number of elementary cycles actually found. The clever part is a *blocking* mechanism that prevents the backtracking search from revisiting vertices along dead-end paths, and that is what avoids the naive combinatorial blow-up. Even so, $C$ itself can grow exponentially with $V$ in dense graphs, so bound the search with `length_bound=` whenever only short cycles are of interest. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two overlapping cycles exist here: the short `A <-> B` back-and-forth, and the longer `A -> B -> C -> A` triangle: ::: {#e5652e2c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # closes A -> B -> C -> A ("B", "A"), # closes A -> B -> A ] ) ) graph.get_cycles() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[2, 3, 1], [2, 1]] ``` ::: ::: Raising `min_length=` filters out the shorter cycle, leaving only the triangle: ::: {#36bdedd0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.get_cycles(min_length=3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [[2, 3, 1]] ``` ::: :::
